content.text: How do we convert sound into electricity and back again? Microphones and loudspeakers are essentially opposite devices—one uses electromagnetic induction to turn sound into electrical signals, while the other uses the motor effect to turn electrical signals into sound. Together, they enable telephones, music systems, and countless audio applications.

A dynamic microphone converts sound energy into electrical energy using electromagnetic induction. A loudspeaker converts electrical energy into sound energy using the motor effect. They are essentially the same device working in reverse.
Both use electromagnetism—they're like motor and generator in audio form.

Louder sound has larger pressure variations
This causes the diaphragm to move further
The coil attached to it moves faster
Faster movement through the magnetic field induces larger voltage

"Louder music needs a more powerful magnet"
— Loudness depends on the electrical signal amplitude. The magnet stays the same.
— Microphones convert sound to electrical signals. Amplification is a separate process.
"Speakers push air out to make sound"
— Speakers push AND pull, creating compressions and rarefactions. Sound is a wave, not a wind.
— Digital microphones still use the same electromagnetic principles, but include an analog-to-digital converter.
— Large speakers are better for bass. Small speakers are better for high frequencies. Most systems use both.

Microphones use electromagnetic induction (generator principle): sound moves the coil, which generates a current. Speakers use the motor effect (motor principle): a current moves the coil, which produces sound. Both require a coil and a permanent magnet.

Microphones and speakers are reciprocal—essentially the same device in reverse

A microphone converts sound (kinetic) energy into electrical energy using electromagnetic induction (generator effect). A loudspeaker converts electrical energy into sound (kinetic) energy using the motor effect. Both use a coil moving in a magnetic field but in opposite directions of energy transfer.

Sound waves cause the diaphragm to vibrate. A coil of wire attached to the diaphragm moves back and forth within the magnetic field of a permanent magnet. This changing position of the coil in the field induces a voltage across it (by electromagnetic induction). The voltage varies with the same frequency and pattern as the original sound wave.

Higher-pitched sound has a higher frequency, meaning more compressions and rarefactions per second. The cone must complete more vibration cycles per second to match, so it must move faster. The frequency of cone vibration equals the frequency of the sound produced.

A loudspeaker contains the same components as a dynamic microphone: a coil attached to a cone/diaphragm in a magnetic field. Tapping or speaking into the cone moves the coil in the field, inducing a small voltage by electromagnetic induction. It is ineffective because the cone is heavy and not optimised for detecting small sound pressure variations.
— The electrical signal frequency matches the sound wave frequency exactly. (recall)

Dynamic: robust, no external power needed, handles loud sounds well; but less sensitive and frequency response is not perfectly flat. Condenser: very sensitive, wide and flat frequency response, excellent detail; but requires external (phantom) power, more fragile, and more expensive.

Connect the loudspeaker terminals to a sensitive voltmeter or oscilloscope. Gently tap or push the cone. The coil moves in the magnetic field, inducing a voltage that registers as a deflection on the voltmeter or a trace on the oscilloscope. This demonstrates electromagnetic induction.
